pineapple.origin: Pineapple leaf fiber (often abbreviated PALF) comes from the long leaves of Ananas comosus (Bromeliaceae). Leaves are a residue of fruit production, and pineapple crowns and leaves make up a large share of plant waste. Indonesia is reported to produce about 23 percent of world pineapples, and fiber is also produced or studied in the Philippines, Thailand and even the Azores. Traditional pina cloth depends on fine fibers scraped from the leaves by hand.
pineapple.structure: PALF has one of the highest cellulose contents among leaf fibers, reported up to about 80 percent or more, with relatively low lignin. Fibers are bundles of very fine elementary cells: enzymatic degumming separates bundles about 10 to 50 microns wide into individual cells of about 5 to 8 microns. Retted Azores fibers measured about 35 to 168 microns in diameter and 1.4 to 7.1 tex. Density is reported at about 1.07 to 1.56 g/cm3, and fiber properties vary strongly along the leaf, from base to tip.
pineapple.process: For pina, fibers are traditionally scraped from the leaves by hand, cleaned, dried, sorted by fineness and joined end to end into yarn for handloom weaving; pina cloth may also combine pineapple fiber with silk or other yarns. Research lines use biological retting (for example about 14 days at 25 C) followed by scraping, or mechanical decorticators, and then degumming with alkali or enzymes such as xylanase, cellulase and pectinase to soften and separate fibers. Suitably treated PALF has been ring spun industrially at up to about 80 percent PALF content and woven on power looms.
pineapple.performance: PALF is strong and stiff: retted Azores fibers showed tensile strength of about 37 to 993 MPa and elongation of about 1 to 4 percent, and some reviews report strengths above 1,000 MPa for fine fibers. Its high cellulose and crystallinity give luster and crispness, the qualities prized in sheer pina cloth. It absorbs moisture like other cellulosics. Enzyme-treated PALF has been naturally dyed with good fastness to washing, perspiration and light in AATCC tests. Degumming improves softness and spinnability but lowers load-bearing capacity.
pineapple.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: PALF burns like other cellulosic fibers. Microscopy shows very fine elementary cells in bundles, finer than most leaf fibers. Pina may be woven with silk or cotton, so a burn or solubility test on a single yarn can mislead; separate yarn systems should be tested. Nonwoven leather alternatives made from pineapple leaf fiber are coated composites and should not be described as woven pineapple cloth.
pineapple.labeling: Pineapple leaf fiber has no Annex I name in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, so EU labels would normally declare it as other fibres with its percentage, and blended silk or cotton must be declared by their own names. In the US, covered textiles must disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303. Coated pineapple-fiber sheet materials contain polymer binders and coatings, so their full composition should be requested from the producer.
pineapple.past: In the Philippines, pina became a prestige textile: a sheer, lustrous handwoven cloth used for formal clothing and fine embroidery. Its hand scraping, sorting and weaving are slow, which has always kept output small and costly. This research pass could not verify specific dates, production centers or heritage listings for pina, so readers should consult official Philippine sources and the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage lists directly. Industrial PALF work is much more recent, with ring-spinning and power-loom trials reported in 2025 studies.

bamboo-bast.origin: Mechanically processed bamboo fiber is taken from the culms of woody bamboos (Poaceae, subfamily Bambusoideae), such as moso bamboo, Phyllostachys edulis, in China. China and India are the largest bamboo producers, with Indonesia reported third. This route differs fundamentally from the far more common bamboo viscose or lyocell, in which bamboo is only a cellulose pulp source that is dissolved and regenerated. Genuinely mechanical bamboo textile fiber is produced in small volumes, and public production data are scarce.
bamboo-bast.structure: Bamboo culm tissue consists of vascular bundles, each sheathed by thick-walled fiber cells, embedded in thin-walled parenchyma. Cellulose makes up roughly 40 to 60 percent of bamboo, and cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin together exceed about 90 percent of dry weight. Native cellulose crystallinity in moso bamboo has been measured at about 40 percent, rising to about 55 to 60 percent after lignin and hemicellulose are removed. Individual fiber cells are short, so textile fiber consists of partly delignified bundles, whose strength depends on how much matrix remains.
bamboo-bast.process: Culms are split, the outer skin and nodes removed, and strips are typically crushed or rolled mechanically. The bundles are then softened by cooking and delignification, using alkali, sulfite, peracid or enzyme treatments, to separate fiber bundles from parenchyma, followed by washing, drying and opening or cutting to spinnable lengths. Drying method matters: oven-dried delignified moso bamboo fibers reached about 850 to 890 MPa in one study, while freeze-dried fibers fell to about 11 to 19 MPa. By contrast, bamboo rayon is made by dissolving pulp in a viscose or solvent process and spinning a new filament.
bamboo-bast.performance: Mechanically separated bamboo fibers are stiff and coarse relative to regenerated fibers; reviews report tensile strengths of about 140 to 800 MPa and elongation of about 1.3 to 7 percent, with densities of about 0.6 to 1.5 g/cm3 depending on porosity. They absorb moisture readily and, when not fully degummed, retain lignin that yellows with light. Claims of intrinsic antibacterial action are frequently made for bamboo textiles; such properties shown in laboratory-modified fibers should not be assumed for commercial fabrics, and any such claim should be backed by test data.
bamboo-bast.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: both bamboo bast and bamboo rayon burn as cellulosics and cannot be distinguished this way. Microscopy is the key test: mechanically processed bamboo shows irregular bundles of lignified cells with lumens, whereas rayon shows uniform manufactured filaments with smooth, often serrated cross-sections. FTIR can reveal aromatic lignin bands (about 1510 and 1600 cm-1) that are largely absent from regenerated cellulose. Many garments sold as bamboo are in fact regenerated cellulose.
bamboo-bast.labeling: In the US, the FTC treats fiber regenerated from bamboo pulp as rayon (or lyocell, a rayon subcategory) under 16 CFR 303.7, and it has repeatedly taken enforcement action, including civil penalties, against sellers who labeled such textiles simply as bamboo. A phrase such as rayon made from bamboo is acceptable only when accurate. Only mechanically processed fiber may be described as bamboo. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 has no Annex I name for bamboo, so regenerated fibers take names such as viscose or lyocell, and mechanical fiber would be other fibres.
bamboo-bast.past: Bamboo has been split, woven and plaited into mats, baskets and structural goods for millennia in East and Southeast Asia, and bamboo pulp has long been used for paper. The textile boom of the 2000s was driven mainly by regenerated bamboo viscose marketed with natural and antibacterial claims, which prompted regulatory scrutiny in the US and elsewhere. Mechanical bamboo fiber production grew as a niche response, and current research focuses on delignification chemistry and drying to obtain stronger, cleaner fibers.
